title: The Five Worst Education Cliches
author: Andrew Old
summary: Andrew Old revives an older post, prompted by UK education secretary Lucy Powell's recent invocation of 'one-size-fits-all' rhetoric, to dissect five stock phrases he argues do the most damage to clear thinking about education policy. Drawing explicitly on Orwell's Politics and the English Language, Old contends that each cliche performs a rhetorical trick that substitutes for an actual argument: 'regurgitating facts' smuggles in a value judgment against recall disguised as a description, 'political football' delegitimizes democratic oversight of education spending as a mere game, 'exam factories' dismisses objective assessment while ignoring that alternatives like coursework more closely resemble factory production, 'educating the whole child' expands teachers' mandate into parenting and therapy without acknowledging the tradeoffs, and 'one size fits all' inverts the usual burden of proof so that advocates of equal treatment must justify themselves while advocates of differentiated, unequal treatment need not. Old's proposed remedy is simple: paraphrase the cliche in plain language and see whether the underlying argument survives.
points: Old applies Orwell's 'prefabricated henhouse' critique of political language specifically to education discourse, arguing that stock phrases let ideologically loaded positions pass as neutral description.

His deconstruction of 'exam factories' turns the metaphor back on its users: he argues coursework and subjective teacher assessment resemble corporate 'performance management' culture more closely than standardized exams do.

The 'political football' analysis makes an explicit democratic-accountability argument: dismissing elected officials' education debates as a 'game' is, in his reading, a move to shift power toward unaccountable bureaucratic and vested interests.

On 'one size fits all,' Old identifies a burden-of-proof inversion as the cliche's real function, it forces defenders of equal treatment to justify themselves while quietly exempting advocates of unequal or selective treatment from the same scrutiny.

His practical test for readers, restate the cliche in your own words and see if the argument survives, offers a portable diagnostic for evaluating loaded language in any policy debate, not just education.
quotes: As soon as certain topics are raised, the concrete melts into the abstract and no one seems able to think of turns of speech that are not hackneyed: prose consists less and less of words chosen for the sake of their meaning, and more and more of phrases tacked together like the sections of a prefabricated henhouse.

Public discourse involving those who have been elected to office, and are subject to public scrutiny, is dismissed as a game by those who would see less democracy in education and more bureaucratic control by unaccountable vested interests.
The greatest irony here is that, in many respects, the alternatives to exams might seem more like factory work. Anyone involved in the "manufacture" of coursework can see that.

If you want education to go beyond the academic, into therapy, social work, entertainment, preaching and parenting, then this cliche can be used to suggest all aspects of a child's life fall in the domain of teachers.

Suddenly, those who support equal rights and equal entitlements for all children are expected to explain why they are ignoring differences between children, while those who support inequality are no longer expected to demonstrate that the differences they perceive justify different and/or unequal treatment.
If you feel inclined to use any of these phrases in education discussion, I challenge you to try to express the same idea in your own words.
